Material Library: India's first phygital specification platform

Knowledge CenterPhygital platform2026

Overview

Material Library is India's first phygital specification platform: a digital workspace and a physical Knowledge Center under one account. Architects, designers, brands, dealers, students and faculty use it to discover, specify and source materials, online and in a library they can walk into.

This case study follows the design from a Figma export to a Swiss newspaper system, across three builds over five months.

The gap between V1 and V3 is five months of one designer working with an AI pair.
Dashboards sharing one shell
8
Routes built
100+
Months, one designer
5

Problem

What I inherited was a Figma export, not a product

The codebase was an export from a Figma Make design: working React components, but every page had its own visual language. The ML side used light backgrounds with glass cards, soft shadows and orange buttons with glows. The KC side was an entirely separate dark theme with violet accents.

Following a name from the feed landed on a different site each time.
Two separate products

ML (orange, light) and KC (violet, dark) looked like different companies. Separate headers and navigation, and no workspace switcher.

Glass card aesthetic

Frosted white panels, soft shadows, orange glows, 16–28px border radii on everything.

Centred layouts

Dark photo heroes with centred text, search bars and pills. No reading direction.

No dashboards

Public pages only: no signed-in experience and no stakeholder workspaces.

The Solution

V2: Eight dashboards, guided tours, a route planner. Still no visual grammar.

V2 was about building the product out. Eight stakeholder dashboards (studio, brand, designer, dealer, student, faculty, institute, customer), each with a sidebar, guided tours, analytics and messaging. The public side expanded with Jobs, Events, Feed and Courses.

The problem: every dashboard had its own sidebar implementation. Ten layouts wrote the same sidebar, mobile drawer, top bar and notification tray from scratch, roughly 2,500 lines saying one thing ten different ways.

What still felt wrong
  • Purple crept in: KC's violet showed up next to ML orange in nav items, progress bars and tour dots.
  • 10 separate sidebars: a fix to one never reached the others.
  • Glass cards everywhere, with no shared card system.
  • "Hi, Ankit 👋": emoji greetings and "COMING SOON" badges that added nothing.

V3: The Swiss system. One typeface, one accent, everything flush left.

V3 is a complete visual reset. The homepage reads like a newspaper, with a live ticker, editorial headlines, "Materials of the Week", specification volumes quarter on quarter, and a carbon counter. Large flush-left headings end with a full stop: Professionals. Events. Sign in.

Every decision removes something: no shadows, no icons in circles, no gradients, no badges. A strict column grid, divided by rules, never by boxes.

Features
  • Newspaper homepage: a publication, not a landing page
  • The full stop: headings as statements, not labels
  • Phygital unified: ML and KC share one account and a header workspace switcher
  • KC dark-first, because showrooms are
Side by side
    V1 → V2
  • 4 public pages → 12+
  • No signed-in experience → 8 stakeholder dashboards
  • No login → demo login with 9 roles
  • Static category cards → discipline sidebar + filter pills
  • No tours → guided onboarding per dashboard
    V2 → V3
  • 10 sidebar implementations → 1 DashboardChrome
  • Glass cards → flat plates with hairline rules
  • Purple + orange → orange only
  • Centred heroes → flush-left headlines with full stops
  • ~2,700 glass-era styles → Swiss tokens
  • 4,800 inline hex values → inversion-filter dark mode
By the numbers
2,500lines of duplicated sidebar code → one DashboardChrome
2,700inline glass-era styles remapped via one override file
4,800inline hex colours across 346 components
245files with a .grid collision, renamed to .ml-grid
8dashboards: one shell, one chrome, one nav file
3CSS scopes preventing cascade collisions

Key Design Decisions

The moments where I said "no, not that"

Me"The brands page looks too similar to professionals. Make it slightly different."
ClaudeDifferentiated it with a warm hero, a magazine-style editor's selection and brand logo avatars. Same data, different editorial treatment.
Me"Fix the spacing on /services." Then: "Still not reflecting that."
ClaudeRan getComputedStyle() and found paddingTop: 0px despite py-12. Root cause: an unlayered .w rule was beating every Tailwind 4 utility, so the CSS architecture had a cascade collision built in.
Me"Remove Settings from the sidebar. Move subscription, billing, API to the avatar dropdown. Fix it for this page first."
ClaudeRemoved Settings from all 8 dashboards and added the account items to the avatar dropdown. One session, because they all share DashboardChrome now.

That last one is the payoff of consolidation. In V2 it would have meant editing 10 separate layout files and hoping none were missed. In V3 it's one component, one file, one session.

I wrote the design grammar into the CSS

I wrote it as rules for myself, not comments for other developers, so I'd stop second-guessing them.

swiss.css— one typeface; weight and size do all the hierarchy
— one accent, used once (the kicker), never as a fill
— no shadows, no icons in circles, no gradients, no badges
— a strict column grid, divided by rules, never by boxes
— everything flush left; numbers in tabular figures
A listing page is a table of things to choose between. The page earns calm by removing, not by arranging.

Key Design Challenges

Designing with an AI pair, in the room where it's used

Claude didn't "generate" this product. I designed it; Claude built what I described, and I corrected what it got wrong. My most common instruction was some variation of "remove that." The real value was speed: a CSS bug that used to take me an hour to diagnose took three minutes.

The work happened in conference rooms at the Knowledge Center, in the physical library while it was being fitted out, and late at night with the code open beside the spreadsheets.

Knowledge Center, Hyderabad · May – October 2026

Holding one system together across
  • 11 material domains
  • 8 stakeholder dashboards
  • A physical library and a digital platform, all under one account

Outcome

A unified phygital platform: a newspaper-style public site, eight dashboards on one shared chrome, and one account across both worlds.

Routes built
100+
Tonnes CO₂e tracked
28,846
Dashboards, one chrome
8
What's next

The same rigour now needs to reach the signed-in experience: the same sidebar rhythm, stat-card anatomy and data-table grid for every role. The other half is bringing KC into the ML dashboards, through a "Visit the library" prompt on a brand's page, workshop schedules for students, and sample requests that bridge online specification with in-person pickup.

One account, one experience, two worlds.

What I Learned

Deleting what took days to build

V2 had guided tours I was proud of. Looked at honestly, they taught people how to use a confusing interface instead of making it less confusing. I had them ripped out and replaced the navigation with a single sidebar component. That was a Wednesday; by Friday, DashboardChrome served all eight dashboards.

Design became editing

Claude over-builds everything: ask for a text label and you get a component with three props, a hover state and an animation. My most-typed phrase was "remove the shadow, remove the border-radius, remove the gradient, just use a rule." But it could scaffold a dashboard in twenty minutes, so my job became editing, not building.

The constraint was the answer

Writing swiss.css meant I could stop asking whether a page needed one more colour or one more card.

The physical space changes the digital design

Watching architects flip through samples in the library showed me the website had to feel like browsing, not searching. That's why the homepage is a newspaper.

The design philosophy came from me. The velocity came from Claude.

Product design: Snigdha Jain · Development: Ankit Kathula · AI partner: Claude (Anthropic)

Everest Systems (now Lensing AI): designing enterprise software that scales

Everest SystemsEnterprise SaaS2024 – 25

Overview

Everest Systems, now Lensing AI, builds an AI-native ERP for finance teams. Over a year as a product designer on a cross-functional team, I owned end-to-end design across four major feature areas (support, procurement, payment collection and billing) while contributing six components to the company's design system, Tenzing.

Every feature decision considers the design system.
Faster issue resolution
42%
Higher customer satisfaction
+63%
Hours saved per month
~202

Problem

Complex financial domains, used every day

Enterprise finance software runs on procurement rules, payment-collection logic and long document lifecycles. These are domains where one confusing state or missing status costs teams hours. Each feature I took on started as reference documents, spreadsheets and PM conversations, not as a brief.

Many lifecycle states

Support tickets move between new, open, closed and re-opened, with edge cases at every transition.

Spreadsheet-shaped data

Procurement data models lived in detailed spreadsheets that had to become usable tables and forms.

Inconsistent components

Status indicators, table headers and error states varied across the platform, which built up design debt.

The Solution

01 · Customer Support Portal

End-to-end workflow design · Enterprise UX

I designed the complete support portal experience: issue creation, tracking, resolution and re-opening. That meant mapping every ticket lifecycle state and making the experience work for both support agents and customers across complex edge cases.

What I did
  • End-to-end flows for creating, viewing and resolving tickets
  • Mapped lifecycle states: new, open, closed, re-opened
  • Re-opening a closed ticket requires a mandatory comment
  • Issue update views so customers can track progress
  • Several rounds of stakeholder feedback on interaction patterns
Impact
  • A complete portal covering every lifecycle state
  • Less support friction through clear status visibility
  • Reusable patterns for status-driven workflows
  • +63% satisfaction, 42% faster resolution within 3 months

02 · Purchase Requests & Purchase Orders

Complex workflow design · Enterprise UX

I designed the end-to-end PR/PO workflow, one of the most complex features in the platform. It required a deep understanding of procurement, extensive collaboration with PMs, and detailed mapping of data from spreadsheets to UI.

What I did
  • Learned the procurement domain through documentation and PM meetings
  • Translated spreadsheet data models into table and form designs
  • Iterated through multiple rounds of design feedback
  • Built detailed component specs for engineering handoff
  • Worked on it continuously for 2+ months alongside other projects
Impact
  • Complex procurement logic turned into a usable interface
  • Patterns reusable for similar document-based workflows
  • Close PM collaboration throughout a multi-month process

03 · Dunning Management

Financial workflow · Stakeholder design

I designed the dunning (payment collection) workflow from reference documents and stakeholder input. That meant understanding the financial logic, going through several feedback rounds with the PM, and presenting to both the team and formal PM reviews.

What I did
  • Turned reference docs and spreadsheets into design concepts
  • Iterated through feedback rounds with PM stakeholders
  • Presented in team meetings for broader feedback
  • Revised after formal PM review
  • Redesigned the subscription component that emerged from this work
Impact
  • Passed PM review after iterative refinement
  • Subscription redesign handed off successfully
  • Showed I can design for complex financial domains

04 · Vendor Bill Revamp

Early exploration · System redesign

I started the early exploration for revamping the vendor bill experience: analysing current pain points and trying new interaction patterns for a core financial workflow.

What I did
  • Led the early exploration phase
  • Analysed the existing experience and found areas to improve
  • Began prototyping new approaches to the billing workflow
Impact
  • Set the design direction for a major upcoming feature
  • Identified key UX improvements for vendor-facing tools

Design System

Tenzing component library

Beyond feature work, I contributed reusable components to Everest's design system, Tenzing, keeping the platform consistent and reducing design debt for future teams.

Status Tag Cell

Standard colour-coded status indicators across all table views.

Tall Header Cell

A flexible header for complex data tables with multi-line content.

Attachment Error

One way to handle file attachment errors, for both URLs and uploads.

Notes Component

In-table and sidebar notes with resizable height and consistent type.

Notification Dot

A visual indicator for notification states, published to Tenzing.

Table Component

Fixed buggy table behaviour and standardised inner shadows and spacing.

My design system process
01
Audit

Find inconsistencies in existing components

02
Design

Create variants in Figma, documented

03
Review

Agree specs with the design system lead and engineers

04
Publish

Publish to Tenzing and update the ZeroHeight docs

Key Design Decisions

Make re-opening deliberate

Re-opening a closed ticket requires a mandatory comment, so agents always know why an issue came back.

Design from the data model

For PR/PO, I worked from the spreadsheets PMs used, so tables and forms matched the real procurement logic rather than an idealised version of it.

Fix the component, not just the screen

The dunning work touched subscriptions, so I redesigned the shared subscription component rather than patching a single flow.

Standardise status everywhere

A single Status Tag Cell gave every table the same visual language for where a record stands.

Key Design Challenges

Learning dense domains quickly

I spent weeks on PR/PO flows in meetings with PMs and studying detailed reference spreadsheets before designing anything.

Many projects in parallel

PR/PO alone ran for 2+ months alongside the support portal, dunning and design-system work.

Getting through review

Financial workflows had to survive several rounds of team and formal PM review before handoff.

Outcome

Six or more features shipped across support, procurement, payment collection and billing, plus six components published to Tenzing and documented in ZeroHeight.

42%faster issue resolution
+63%customer satisfaction
−35%missed alerts after the Notification Center redesign
2×Notes engagement, +24% DAU
−32%user confusion in procurement flows
~202hours saved per month

What I Learned

Deep domain understanding comes first

I invest time in complex business domains, from procurement to dunning logic, through documentation, stakeholder meetings and conversations across teams.

"I spent weeks understanding PR/PO flows through meetings with PMs and detailed reference spreadsheets before designing."
Design in tight feedback loops

I present to PMs, get input from engineers, revise and present again. I don't disappear and come back with a big reveal.

"The dunning flow went through multiple rounds of team meetings and PM reviews before handoff, and each round strengthened the design."
Systems-level thinking

I fix inconsistencies when I find them, create reusable components and document patterns for the team.

"While building features, I contributed 6+ components to Tenzing and maintained the ZeroHeight documentation."

Flow Twin: your voice, working for you

Wispr FlowConcept + prototype2026

Overview

Wispr Flow helps people type faster by speaking. Flow Twin proposes a new kind of product: a narrow, work-only AI twin, built passively from how a person already talks in Flow and deployed through a single WhatsApp link. It answers routine questions in your voice and hands the rest to you.

How might we turn Wispr Flow from a tool that helps you type faster into a platform that lets your voice keep working after you've stopped talking?
Stages in the user journey
7
Of inbound the twin could handle
~70%
App downloads needed
0

Problem

The signal is already there, and it's being thrown away

I've lived in two markets that treat technology very differently. In the US, the iPhone and the App Store are the baseline assumption. In India that assumption breaks: Android dominates, app fatigue is real, and nobody downloads another tool just to try something. But almost everyone is on WhatsApp, and not just personally. For many working people in India, WhatsApp is where client follow-ups, vendor negotiations and introductions happen.

A few days into using Wispr Flow, I noticed it was sitting on extraordinarily rich data: unscripted speech that captures how a person actually thinks. Every dictated email and Slack reply carried vocabulary, reasoning and tone. At the end of each session, it disappeared.

Around the same time I found Delphi, which builds an AI version of you from content you upload. Most people never upload consistently enough, so the model stays shallow.

Wispr Flow already has what Delphi is trying to manufacture. It's just not being used.
Knowledge doesn't scale, and neither does time

Professionals protect their time by raising prices, which puts their expertise out of reach for the people who most need it. The high-stakes work still needs the human, but the roughly 70% of inbound that's repetitive or exploratory could be handled by something that genuinely sounds like them.

The Solution

A third privacy state that doesn't exist yet

Wispr Flow has two modes today: default (data may improve Wispr's models) and Privacy Mode (zero retention). Flow Twin needs a third, and naming it clearly is half the design work.

"I want my data retained, not to train Wispr's models, but to train my own twin. I own the output. I control the deployment."

Consent becomes a feature unlock rather than a terms-of-service checkbox. It's a dedicated screen, not a modal, that states what's used (transcripts, not audio), what it builds, who controls it, and what Wispr gets (nothing).

The journey: passive build, active deploy

1 · Discovery

After two weeks of use, a banner appears in the dashboard: "Your voice has been working. Want to put it to work for others?" It invites curiosity rather than pushing.

2 · Opt-in

A full consent screen: transparent, unhurried and explicit. "Train my Flow Twin" is a separate toggle from every other privacy control.

3 · The recognition moment

When a confidence threshold is reached, not after a fixed timer, the user sees five or six sample questions with draft answers in their voice and can mark each one "sounds like me" or "not quite." This is the moment that creates ownership.

4 · Scope and guardrails

The user defines what the twin handles, what it always escalates (pricing, contracts, ready-to-hire, anything new) and the escalation message. Knowing when not to answer is the product's real intelligence.

5 · WhatsApp deployment

One link and a QR code for an email signature, LinkedIn bio or WhatsApp status. Tapping it opens a WhatsApp chat with the twin, with no download and no account. Every reply carries "Snigdha's Flow Twin · Wispr Flow", so every conversation is both useful and an advert for Wispr.

6 · Live triage and the learning loop

A weekly digest, not a stream of notifications, shows what was handled, what was escalated and what people keep asking. Answering an escalated query trains the twin for next time.

7 · Confidence calibration

Weak topics show up as invitations, not errors: "People keep asking about your pricing. Your twin isn't confident here yet. Want to train it?"

Key Design Decisions

Passive training, not manual curation

Every tool in this space fails on activation energy: people intend to upload content, and they don't. Flow Twin builds the model as a byproduct of something people already do every day, with no change in behaviour required.

WhatsApp, not a new app

The distribution channel is the product decision. WhatsApp is already open, and the conversation is already happening there.

Narrow scope, not a general avatar

People speak differently to clients and friends. A twin that tries to represent the whole person fails at the edges. A Work Twin only claims professional inbound. The constraint is the feature.

The recognition moment is the real product

Everything before it is infrastructure; everything after it is retention.

Access design, not automation

It extends a professional's knowledge to people who can't afford their time, while their time stays reserved for what genuinely needs them.

What It Unlocks

Not a feature, a category shift

Dictation speed is a low ceiling, and utilities get commoditised. A twin that sounds like you, that your contacts already know how to reach, is something you don't switch away from.

DimensionTodayWith Flow Twin
CategoryDictation / productivityIdentity infrastructure
RetentionSpeed of dictationAn irreplaceable personal model
Pricing₹320/moProposed ₹1,500–5,000/mo
Viral loopNone, the tool is invisibleEvery twin link is a Wispr ad
India GTMApp downloadWhatsApp-native, referral-led
Risks I'd design around
Identity liability

The twin will sometimes be wrong, so AI disclosure has to be in every reply.

Consent must be felt

If anyone feels they enabled this by accident, the trust damage can't be undone.

Cold start

Gate activation on confidence, not time, and set expectations early.

DPDP Act

Get consent and data ownership right from the start and turn compliance into an advantage.

Reflection

I sent this concept directly to Tanay Kothari, Wispr Flow's CEO, whom I'd met at Open Atlas Summit in 2025. Unsolicited concepts only land when they have a genuine point of view, and I wanted this one to.

The best design problems aren't the ones where something is broken. They're the ones where something is being wasted.

Distribution is a design decision. Consent is a product feature. The strongest case for any concept is the person it actually helps.

Independent concept · not affiliated with Wispr Flow

Patch It: Inspect Element edits that survive a refresh

Side projectChrome extension2026

Overview

Patch It is a small Chrome extension that keeps the cosmetic changes you make in Inspect Element, so a refresh doesn't send you back to square one. I built it with AI tools to solve a problem I kept hitting as a product designer.

Who doesn't hate that moment?

Problem

One accidental refresh, and every tweak is gone

As a product designer, I want to make recurring cosmetic changes directly in the browser. But the minute you start editing in Inspect Element and hit refresh by mistake, everything goes back to the way it was.

The Solution

An extension that remembers the patch

So, out of frustration and my love for AI, I built a Chrome extension that solves it. I don't want to keep redoing the same cosmetic changes again and again. Tada.

How it works
  • Pick any element on the page; its selector path shows at the top
  • Edit its style or content in the Style and Content tabs
  • Every edit is saved as a patch you can switch on or off
  • Remove a patch with one click
Demo

The demo video shows the extension keeping edits after the page reloads.

Limitations

Desktop only, for now

It works on a desktop or laptop, but the changes don't show up on a phone. So this is a work in progress.

I don't want to keep redoing the cosmetic changes again and again.

AI Slop Detector: LinkedIn authenticity

Side projectChrome extension2026

Overview

Slop Detector sits on top of the LinkedIn feed and gives each post an authenticity score from 0 to 100. Posts that score below your threshold are collapsed, so real people's stories rise to the top.

Real person, real story, or textbook AI output?
Score bands
5
Point authenticity scale
0–100
Default hide threshold
30

Problem

A feed where it's hard to tell who's actually talking

More and more of the LinkedIn feed reads like it was generated rather than written. Telling a real story from templated AI output takes attention, post after post.

The Solution

Score, then let the reader decide what to see

A badge on every post

Each post gets a badge with its band and score, for example "Likely Human 85". Hovering it shows why: the signals Claude found, such as personal anecdotes and casual language on the human side, or emoji bullets on the AI side, plus a confidence level.

Slop folds away, but stays one tap from view

A post below the threshold collapses to a single line, for example "AI Slop · Score: 28/100", with a "Show anyway" button.

A clear score guide
ScoreBandMeans
80–100HumanReal person, real story
60–79Likely humanMostly authentic
40–59MixedMaybe AI-assisted
20–39Likely AIProbably generated
0–19AI slopTextbook AI output
A hide threshold you control

A slider from "Never hide" to "Hide all AI". At the default of 30, likely-AI posts are collapsed rather than removed.

A live tally

Counters for posts scanned, human and slop (8, 4 and 3 in the demo), plus an on/off toggle at the top.

Bring your own key

Scoring runs on Claude through the user's own Anthropic API key, saved in the extension.

Watch the Slop Detector demo

Opens the video on LinkedIn.

linkedin ↗

Key Design Decisions

Collapse, don't delete

Low-scoring posts fold away with their score and a "Show anyway" button, so the reader stays in control.

Show the reasoning

A score alone asks for trust. The hover explanation lists the signals behind it and a confidence level, so the reader can judge for themselves.

Five plain-language bands

Every number comes with a short phrase, like "Real person, real story", so the score is easy to read at a glance.

One adjustable threshold

One slider instead of a settings page: tolerance for AI content is a personal choice.
